q: A by-product is sold for Rs 60,000. The estimated profit on its sale is 20 per cent of the sales value, its selling and distribution expenses are Rs 4,000 and the cost of its further processing after the split-off point is Rs 14,000. Under the reverse cost method, the amount credited to the main process account for the by-product is:
e: Reverse cost credit = sales Rs 60,000 - profit 20% Rs 12,000 - selling expenses Rs 4,000 - further processing Rs 14,000 = Rs 30,000.

q: In batch costing, the Economic Batch Quantity is fixed at the level at which:

options.A: The material cost per unit of the batch is the lowest
options.B: The selling price of the batch just covers its prime cost
options.C: The total profit earned on all the batches of the year is the maximum
options.D: The total set-up cost for the year and the total carrying cost for the year are equal to each other

e: Economic Batch Quantity is set where total yearly set-up cost equals total yearly carrying cost, minimising their combined total.

q: Retention money withheld by the contractee on the value of work certified is, in the books of the contractor, in substance:

options.A: A profit earned on the contract, to be credited at once to the Profit and Loss Account
options.B: An amount still receivable from the contractee, remaining locked up in the contract work until it is released after satisfactory completion
options.C: A loss on the contract, to be written off in the year of withholding itself
options.D: A liability of the contractor towards his sub-contractors on the work

e: Retention money is still receivable from the contractee, locked up in the contract work until released after satisfactory completion, not profit or loss yet.

q: In the cost ledger, the Finished Stock Ledger Control Account is credited with:

options.A: The cost of the goods sold during the period, transferred to the Cost of Sales Account
options.B: The materials purchased for the factory during the period
options.C: The wages accrued but not yet paid at the end of the period
options.D: The selling and distribution expenses incurred during the period

e: The Finished Stock Ledger Control Account is credited with the cost of goods sold, transferred to the Cost of Sales Account.

q: The total operating cost of a goods transport service for a period is Rs 18,40,000 and the service performed during the period is 4,60,000 tonne-kilometres. The operating cost per tonne-kilometre is:
e: Cost per tonne-km = Rs 18,40,000 / 4,60,000 tonne-km = Rs 4.00.

q: The output of a process is transferred to the next process at cost plus 25 per cent on cost. For working out the unrealised profit contained in a closing stock valued at this transfer price, the profit element is:

options.A: One-fifth, that is, 25/125, of the transfer price of the stock
options.B: One-fourth, that is, 25/100, of the transfer price of the stock
options.C: One-third of the cost of the stock to the receiving process
options.D: The whole of the difference between the transfer price and the selling price

e: Profit of 25% on cost is 25/125, i.e. one-fifth, of the transfer price, which is the profit element in stock valued at transfer price.

q: The apportionment of joint costs among joint products is necessary mainly for:

options.A: Deciding whether a joint product should be sold at the split-off point or processed further
options.B: Fixing the price at which each joint product must be sold in the market
options.C: Valuing the stocks of the joint products and measuring the profit earned on each of them
options.D: Determining the total joint cost to be incurred on the common process

e: Joint cost apportionment is needed mainly to value stocks of joint products and measure profit on each; split-off decisions use incremental analysis instead.

q: The annual demand for a component is 12,800 units. The set-up cost is Rs 200 per batch and the carrying cost is Rs 8 per unit per year. Using EBQ = sqrt(2DS/C), the Economic Batch Quantity is:

options.A: 566 units
options.B: 800 units
options.C: 1,131 units
options.D: 400 units

e: EBQ = sqrt(2 x 12,800 x Rs 200 / Rs 8) = sqrt(6,40,000) = 800 units.

q: In the cost accounts, the administration overheads of a factory have been over-absorbed. In a reconciliation starting with the profit as per the cost accounts, this over-absorption is dealt with by:

options.A: Deducting it from the cost profit, because excess overhead has been charged in the cost accounts
options.B: Ignoring it, because administration overheads do not enter the cost accounts
options.C: Showing it only in the financial accounts of the enterprise
options.D: Adding it to the cost profit, because the cost accounts have charged more overhead than was actually incurred

e: Starting from cost profit, over-absorbed administration overhead is added back, because cost accounts charged more overhead than was actually incurred.

q: Scrap, as distinguished from a by-product, is:

options.A: A product which is deliberately manufactured along with the main product
options.B: A joint product which can be sold only after further processing
options.C: The material residue discarded in the course of manufacture, which has a comparatively low realisable value and is not produced as a planned secondary product
options.D: The finished stock of the factory remaining unsold at the end of the year

e: Scrap is material residue discarded in manufacture, of comparatively low realisable value and not a planned secondary product, unlike a by-product.

q: On a contract, the value of work certified exceeds one-half of the contract price. The notional profit is Rs 1,20,000 and cash received from the contractee is 75 per cent of the work certified. The profit to be credited to the Profit and Loss Account is:
e: Work certified exceeds half the contract price, so profit credited = 2/3 x Rs 1,20,000 x (cash received / work certified 75%) = Rs 60,000.

q: Factory overheads absorbed into production during a period fall short of the factory overheads actually incurred, and no supplementary absorption rate is applied. The balance so left in the Production Overhead Control Account is disposed of by transferring it to:

options.A: The Stores Ledger Control Account
options.B: The Work-in-Progress Ledger Control Account of the next period
options.C: The balance sheet, as a permanent asset of the factory
options.D: The Costing Profit and Loss Account, as an under-absorption of overheads

e: Under-absorbed factory overhead left in the Production Overhead Control Account is transferred to the Costing Profit and Loss Account.

q: Where a by-product recovered in a process requires further processing before it can be sold, the costs incurred on that further processing are accumulated in:

options.A: The main process account itself, as a part of the cost of the main product
options.B: A separate By-product Process Account opened for that by-product
options.C: The general Profit and Loss Account as a period expense
options.D: The Abnormal Loss Account of the process in which it arises

e: Further processing costs of a by-product are accumulated in a separate By-product Process Account, not in the main process account.

q: The output of a process is transferred to the next process at a price which carries a profit of 20 per cent on the transfer price. The closing stock of the receiving process, valued at the transfer price, is Rs 1,50,000. The unrealised profit contained in this stock is:
e: Profit is 20% on transfer price, so unrealised profit in stock = 20% x Rs 1,50,000 = Rs 30,000.

q: In the operating costing of a water supply undertaking, the cost unit most commonly used for expressing the cost of the service is the cost:

options.A: Per consumer connected to the supply system
options.B: Per kilometre of pipeline laid by the undertaking
options.C: Per employee engaged in the water works
options.D: Per kilolitre, that is, per 1,000 litres, of water supplied

e: For a water supply undertaking, cost is commonly expressed per kilolitre, i.e. per 1,000 litres of water supplied.

q: The profit as per the cost accounts of a factory is Rs 2,50,000. Factory overheads have been under-absorbed in the cost accounts by Rs 22,000, and interest of Rs 15,000 received on investments has been credited in the financial accounts only. The profit as per the financial accounts is:
e: Financial profit = Rs 2,50,000 - under-absorbed overhead Rs 22,000 + investment interest Rs 15,000 (financial only) = Rs 2,43,000.

q: A joint cost of Rs 3,00,000 is to be apportioned between joint products A and B by the contribution method. The contribution of A is Rs 2,00,000 and the contribution of B is Rs 1,00,000. The share of joint cost borne by product A is:
e: A's share = contribution ratio 2,00,000 / 3,00,000 x Rs 3,00,000 joint cost = Rs 2,00,000.

q: In the cost ledger, the Stores Ledger Control Account shows an opening balance of Rs 95,000. During the period, materials purchased amounted to Rs 3,85,000, materials returned from production departments to the stores amounted to Rs 18,000, materials issued to production amounted to Rs 4,10,000 and materials returned to suppliers amounted to Rs 12,000. The closing balance of the account is:
Materials issued for one contract are transferred, before use, to another contract of the same contractor. The document on the basis of which the transfer is recorded in the contract accounts is the:

options.A: Architect's certificate issued for the receiving contract
options.B: Purchase invoice received from the supplier of the materials
options.C: Contractee's payment advice for the transferring contract
options.D: Material Transfer Note prepared for the movement of the materials between the two contracts

e: Materials transferred between contracts are recorded on a Material Transfer Note prepared for the movement between the two contracts.

q: In a process, 9,000 units are completed and transferred to the next process during a period. The closing work-in-progress is 2,000 units, which are complete as to materials but only 30% complete as to conversion costs, and there was no opening work-in-progress. The equivalent production in respect of conversion costs is:

options.A: 11,000 units
options.B: 9,300 units
options.C: 10,400 units
options.D: 9,600 units

e: Conversion equivalent production = completed 9,000 + closing WIP 2,000 x 30% = 9,000 + 600 = 9,600 units, there being no opening WIP.

q: In the financial justification of a railway works proposal, the earnings taken into account for judging remunerativeness are best described as:

options.A: The additional earnings expected to arise from the work, after meeting the additional working expenses attributable to it
options.B: The gross earnings of the whole zonal railway for the year
options.C: The total originating earnings of the stations served by the work, without deducting any expenses
options.D: The book value of the assets created by the work

e: For financial justification, earnings are the additional earnings expected from the work after meeting the additional working expenses attributable to it.

q: A work is described as unremunerative when:

options.A: It is completed after the year in which it was sanctioned
options.B: Its anticipated rate of return falls short of the prescribed test of remunerativeness
options.C: It requires land to be acquired before execution can begin
options.D: Its estimate includes departmental charges

e: A work is unremunerative when its anticipated rate of return falls short of the prescribed test of remunerativeness.

q: A crossing station is estimated to cost Rs 6 crore and is expected to yield net annual earnings of Rs 78 lakh after meeting the additional working expenses. Its anticipated rate of return, judged against the prescribed 10% test, is:

options.A: 7.8%; the work is unremunerative
options.B: 13%; the work is remunerative
options.C: 10%; the work just fails the test
options.D: 15%; the work is unremunerative

e: Rate of return = Rs 78 lakh / Rs 6 crore = 78 / 600 = 13%, which exceeds the 10% test, so the work is remunerative.

q: Financial appraisal and economic appraisal of the same railway project differ principally in that economic appraisal:

options.A: Ignores the capital cost of the project altogether
options.B: Uses accounting profit in place of cash flows
options.C: Is carried out only after the project has been completed
options.D: Takes into account wider benefits and costs to the economy and society, in addition to the receipts and outgoings of the Railways themselves

e: Economic appraisal takes into account wider benefits and costs to the economy and society, beyond the Railways' own receipts and outgoings.

q: In a social cost-benefit appraisal of a railway project, benefits such as saving in travelling time, reduction in road accidents and relief of road congestion are:

options.A: Excluded because they do not accrue to the Railways in cash
options.B: Treated as depreciation of the project assets
options.C: Taken into account as part of the economic benefits of the project
options.D: Counted only if the project is financially remunerative

e: Time saving, fewer road accidents and less road congestion are economic benefits and are taken into account in social cost-benefit appraisal.

q: A goods shed improvement is estimated to cost Rs 3 crore. Its expected gross earnings are Rs 95 lakh a year and its expected additional working expenses are Rs 62 lakh a year. Its anticipated rate of return is:
e: Net earnings = Rs 95 lakh - Rs 62 lakh = Rs 33 lakh. Return = 33 / 300 = 11% on the Rs 3 crore cost.

q: The Financial Internal Rate of Return (FIRR) of a railway project measures the return:

options.A: To the national economy, including all external benefits
options.B: To society after adding network effects on other lines
options.C: To the exchequer by way of taxes alone
options.D: To the Railways themselves, from the project's own receipts and outgoings

e: FIRR measures the return to the Railways themselves from the project's own receipts and outgoings, excluding wider economic effects.

q: The Economic Internal Rate of Return (EIRR) of a project is ordinarily expected to differ from its Financial Internal Rate of Return because EIRR:

options.A: Includes social and external benefits and costs, and treats taxes and subsidies as transfer payments rather than real costs or benefits
options.B: Is worked out without discounting any cash flow
options.C: Is based on book profits instead of cash flows
options.D: Excludes the capital cost from the computation

e: EIRR differs because it includes social and external benefits and costs and treats taxes and subsidies as transfer payments, not real costs or benefits.

q: A yard remodelling proposal requires an initial outlay of Rs 9,60,000. The present value of its expected cash inflows is Rs 11,04,000. Its Net Present Value is:
e: NPV = present value of inflows Rs 11,04,000 - initial outlay Rs 9,60,000 = (+) Rs 1,44,000.

q: The Modified Economic Internal Rate of Return (MEIRR), as distinguished from the ordinary EIRR, additionally brings into account:

options.A: The depreciation charged in the books of account
options.B: Network effects, that is, the effect of the project on earnings and costs elsewhere on the railway system
options.C: The interest paid during construction only
options.D: The dividend payable to the general exchequer

e: MEIRR additionally brings in network effects, i.e. the project's effect on earnings and costs elsewhere on the railway system, beyond ordinary EIRR.

q: Passenger amenity works and labour welfare works are generally treated, in the matter of financial justification, as:

options.A: Works that must each show the full prescribed rate of return separately
options.B: Works whose cost is met entirely from the Depreciation Reserve Fund
options.C: Works that can be executed without any sanction
options.D: Exceptions to the ordinary requirement of financial justification

e: Passenger amenity and labour welfare works are generally exceptions to the ordinary requirement of financial justification.

q: A water recycling plant costs Rs 8,40,000 and is expected to give a uniform net cash inflow of Rs 2,10,000 at the end of each year. Its payback period is:

options.A: 3 years
options.B: 3.5 years
options.C: 5 years
options.D: 4 years

e: Payback = initial cost / uniform annual inflow = Rs 8,40,000 / Rs 2,10,000 = 4 years.

q: Where a work that is itself exempt from financial justification forms part of a larger remunerative scheme, sound appraisal requires that:

options.A: The exempt portion be excluded from the cost of the scheme
options.B: The work be split into separate proposals to avoid justification
options.C: The scheme as a whole be financially justified, including the exempt portion
options.D: Only the exempt portion be justified

e: Where an exempt work forms part of a larger remunerative scheme, the scheme as a whole must be financially justified including the exempt portion.

q: A post-completion financial review of a work, comparing the actual earnings and costs with those anticipated at the time of sanction, is carried out primarily to:

options.A: Fix responsibility for the original estimate and draw lessons for the appraisal of future proposals
options.B: Reopen the sanction accorded to the completed work
options.C: Revise the classification of the expenditure already incurred
options.D: Avoid the need for a completion report

e: Post-completion review compares actual earnings and costs with those anticipated at sanction, to fix responsibility and draw lessons for future appraisal.

q: A project costing Rs 7,20,000 yields net cash inflows of Rs 1,80,000 in Year 1, Rs 2,40,000 in Year 2 and Rs 3,00,000 in Year 3. Its payback period is:

options.A: 2 years
options.B: 2.5 years
options.C: 3 years
options.D: 3.5 years

e: Cumulative inflows: Year 1 Rs 1,80,000, Year 2 Rs 4,20,000, Year 3 Rs 7,20,000, exactly recovering the cost, so payback is 3 years.

q: In sensitivity analysis of a works proposal, the appraiser examines:

options.A: Only the effect of a change in the discount rate, ignoring traffic and cost changes
options.B: Whether the executing agency has enough staff to complete the work
options.C: How the viability of the project changes when key assumptions such as traffic earnings, capital cost or working expenses vary
options.D: The sensitivity of the estimate to the spelling of the work's name

e: Sensitivity analysis examines how project viability changes when key assumptions like traffic earnings, capital cost or working expenses vary.

q: A proposal whose Net Present Value remains positive even when the anticipated earnings are reduced and the capital cost is increased within reasonable limits is best described as:

options.A: Financially fragile
options.B: Dependent on a single assumption
options.C: Due for abandonment at the first review
options.D: Financially robust to adverse variations in its key assumptions

e: A project whose NPV stays positive despite reduced earnings and increased capital cost within reasonable limits is financially robust to adverse variations.

q: An amount of Rs 6,00,000 is receivable at the end of Year 2. The present value factor for Year 2 at 10% is 0.826. The present value of the amount is:
e: Present value = Rs 6,00,000 x 0.826 = Rs 4,95,600.

q: The break-even level of traffic for a new facility is the level at which:

options.A: The capital cost of the facility is fully recovered in the first year
options.B: The additional earnings from the facility just cover its additional working expenses and the return required on its cost, as framed for the appraisal
options.C: The facility begins to be used by any traffic at all
options.D: The gross earnings of the facility equal its capital cost

e: Break-even traffic is the level where additional earnings just cover additional working expenses and the required return on cost, as framed for appraisal.

q: A facility involves an annual fixed burden of Rs 9,00,000 for the purpose of a break-even computation and earns a contribution of Rs 45 per unit of traffic handled. The break-even volume is:

options.A: 15,000 units
options.B: 20,000 units
options.C: 18,000 units
options.D: 25,000 units

e: Break-even volume = fixed burden / contribution per unit = Rs 9,00,000 / Rs 45 = 20,000 units.

q: A project will give a net cash inflow of Rs 1,20,000 at the end of each year for 4 years. The cumulative present value (annuity) factor for 4 years at 10% is 3.170. The present value of the inflows is:
e: Present value = annual inflow x annuity factor = Rs 1,20,000 x 3.170 = Rs 3,80,400.

q: In estimating the earnings of a proposed work, a prudent financial justification should:

options.A: Adopt the most optimistic traffic forecast available so that the work passes the test
options.B: Ignore the effect of the work on the earnings of connecting lines
options.C: Base the estimate on realistic, supportable traffic and earnings assumptions, avoiding deliberate overstatement
options.D: Assume that working expenses will not rise after the work is opened

e: Prudent justification bases earnings on realistic, supportable traffic assumptions, avoiding deliberate overstatement to pass the test.

q: A shortcoming commonly pointed out in the financial appraisal of railway proposals as actually practised is:

options.A: That discounted cash flow is used for every small work
options.B: That all proposals are subjected to post-completion review without exception
options.C: That anticipated earnings are never estimated at all
options.D: That earnings tend to be overestimated and costs underestimated, with little systematic post-completion comparison against the original justification

e: In practice earnings tend to be overestimated and costs underestimated, with little systematic post-completion comparison against the original justification.

q: The present value of the future cash inflows of a project is Rs 15,60,000 and its initial investment is Rs 13,00,000. Its Profitability Index is:
e: Profitability Index = present value of inflows / initial investment = Rs 15,60,000 / Rs 13,00,000 = 1.20.

q: In economic appraisal, market prices of inputs are sometimes adjusted to shadow prices principally in order to:

options.A: Reflect the real cost or value of the resources to the economy where market prices are distorted
options.B: Make every project appear financially remunerative
options.C: Avoid discounting the cash flows of the project
options.D: Replace the need for estimating traffic altogether

e: Shadow prices adjust distorted market prices to reflect the real cost or value of resources to the economy in economic appraisal.

q: A doubling project is expected to relieve congestion and allow additional trains to be run on a connected section, raising earnings there as well. In a complete appraisal, these connected earnings should be:

options.A: Ignored, since they do not arise on the doubled section itself
options.B: Counted twice, once on each section
options.C: Brought into account as part of the benefits attributable to the project, without double counting
options.D: Treated as a capital receipt of the connected section

e: Connected earnings raised on other sections by the project are brought into account as benefits attributable to it, without double counting.

q: The Net Present Value of a project is (+) Rs 30,000 at a discount rate of 11% and (-) Rs 20,000 at a discount rate of 16%. By interpolation, its Internal Rate of Return is approximately:
Where a work fails the test of financial remunerativeness but is proposed on safety or strategic grounds, the justification placed on record should:

options.A: Show the work as remunerative by suitably adjusting the earnings
options.B: State plainly that the work is financially unremunerative and record the non-financial grounds on which it is nevertheless proposed
options.C: Omit any mention of the rate of return
options.D: Split the work into smaller parts until each part passes the test

e: For a work failing the financial test but proposed on safety or strategic grounds, the record must state plainly it is unremunerative and record those grounds.

q: The discounted cash flow technique is preferred to the simple rate of return on initial cost for appraising long-life railway works mainly because it:

options.A: Requires no estimate of future earnings
options.B: Takes into account the time value of money and the cash flows over the whole life of the project
options.C: Ignores the timing of receipts and outgoings
options.D: Always gives a higher rate of return than the simple method

e: Discounted cash flow is preferred because it takes into account the time value of money and cash flows over the whole life of the project.

q: An investment of Rs 9,00,000 is expected to yield an average annual profit after depreciation of Rs 1,08,000. Its Average Rate of Return on the initial investment is:
e: Average Rate of Return = average annual profit / initial investment = Rs 1,08,000 / Rs 9,00,000 x 100 = 12%.

q: In a discounted cash flow justification, the initial cost of a work should include:

options.A: The full capital outlay required to bring the work into use, including the additional working capital where the framing of the appraisal so requires
options.B: Only the cost of materials, excluding labour and supervision
options.C: Only expenditure incurred in the first financial year
options.D: The book value of the assets that the work replaces, in every case

e: The initial cost must cover the full capital outlay to bring the work into use, including additional working capital where the appraisal requires it, not just materials or first-year spend.

q: A rise in the anticipated working expenses of a proposed work, its earnings and capital cost remaining unchanged, will:

options.A: Raise its anticipated rate of return
options.B: Leave its anticipated rate of return unchanged
options.C: Reduce its anticipated net earnings and therefore lower its rate of return and Net Present Value
options.D: Improve its payback period

e: Higher working expenses with unchanged earnings and cost reduce net earnings, so the rate of return and NPV both fall.

q: A project involves an initial outlay of Rs 5,00,000. The discounted (present) values of its cash inflows are Rs 1,60,000 in Year 1, Rs 1,80,000 in Year 2 and Rs 1,70,000 in Year 3. Its discounted payback period is approximately:

options.A: 1.9 years
options.B: 2.9 years
options.C: 3.0 years exactly at the start of Year 3
options.D: More than 4 years

e: Cumulative discounted inflows are Rs 1,60,000 after Year 1 and Rs 3,40,000 after Year 2; Rs 1,60,000 more is needed from Year 3's Rs 1,70,000, giving about 2 + 160/170 = 2.9 years.

q: The financial justification of a proposal for residential quarters rests, at the concept level, on:

options.A: The operating ratio of the zonal railway
options.B: The dividend payable on the capital invested in them
options.C: The savings expected in the wages of the staff housed
options.D: The assessed rent recoverable for the quarters, which is required to yield the prescribed return on their cost

e: Residential quarters are justified by the assessed rent recoverable for them, which must yield the prescribed return on their capital cost.

q: Earnings of a proposed new line that arise because the line feeds traffic on to an existing line are an illustration of benefits captured by:

options.A: Financial appraisal confined strictly to the new line's own receipts
options.B: Economic appraisal that takes network effects into account
options.C: The payback method applied without discounting
options.D: A post-completion audit conducted before the line is opened

e: Traffic fed on to an existing line is a network benefit beyond the new line's own receipts, so it is captured by economic appraisal, not a narrow financial appraisal.

q: The present value of the benefits of a project is Rs 33,60,000 and the present value of its costs is Rs 28,00,000. Its benefit-cost ratio is:
e: Benefit-cost ratio = PV of benefits / PV of costs = 33,60,000 / 28,00,000 = 1.20.

q: A project whose benefit-cost ratio is less than 1 should, on that criterion alone, be regarded as:

options.A: Worth accepting, because its costs exceed its benefits
options.B: Automatically eligible for execution as a welfare work
options.C: Not worthwhile, because the present value of its benefits falls short of the present value of its costs
options.D: Equivalent to a project with a positive Net Present Value

e: A benefit-cost ratio below 1 means the PV of benefits is less than the PV of costs, so the project is not worthwhile on that criterion and cannot have a positive NPV.

q: Residential quarters are built at a cost of Rs 1.2 crore. The annual assessed rent recoverable for them is Rs 7,20,000. The yield by way of assessed rent on the cost is:
e: Yield = annual assessed rent / cost = 7,20,000 / 1,20,00,000 = 0.06, that is 6 percent.

q: Viability gap funding for a project that is economically worthwhile but not fully financially viable is intended to:

options.A: Replace the need for any financial appraisal of the project
options.B: Meet the whole capital cost of the project as a grant
options.C: Bridge the gap between the project's cost and what it can support financially, so that it can be taken up, commonly with private participation
options.D: Guarantee the contractor's profit on the works contract

e: Viability gap funding bridges the gap between a project's cost and what it can support financially, making an economically worthwhile project taken up, often with private participation.

q: The Net Present Value of a project is (+) Rs 90,000 and the present value of its cash inflows is Rs 18,00,000. The percentage by which the cash inflows can fall before the Net Present Value becomes zero is:
e: The fall that wipes out NPV is NPV / PV of inflows = 90,000 / 18,00,000 = 0.05, that is 5 percent.

q: A project shows an annual accounting profit after depreciation of Rs 2,10,000. The depreciation charged in arriving at this profit is Rs 70,000. The annual net cash inflow from the project is:
e: Depreciation is a non-cash charge, so net cash inflow = accounting profit + depreciation = 2,10,000 + 70,000 = Rs 2,80,000.

q: A facility will bring additional earnings of Rs 5,60,000 a year and will involve additional working expenses of Rs 3,85,000 a year. It is estimated to cost Rs 17,50,000. Its anticipated rate of return is:
A project costing Rs 7,00,000 has a present value of operating cash inflows of Rs 6,40,000 and a present value of salvage value of Rs 1,00,000. Its Net Present Value is:
e: NPV = PV of operating inflows + PV of salvage - cost = 6,40,000 + 1,00,000 - 7,00,000 = (+) Rs 40,000.

q: A work is expected to yield net annual earnings of Rs 60 lakh. At an estimated cost of Rs 5 crore its rate of return is 12%. If the estimated cost rises to Rs 6 crore with the same earnings, its rate of return becomes:
e: Rate of return = net earnings / cost = 60,00,000 / 6,00,00,000 = 10 percent when the cost rises to Rs 6 crore.

q: A project has a Net Present Value of Rs 3,04,000 and the cumulative present value (annuity) factor for its life at the cost of capital is 3.800. Its equivalent annual annuity is:
e: Equivalent annual annuity = NPV / annuity factor = 3,04,000 / 3.800 = Rs 80,000.

q: In a budgetary control organisation, the budget committee is headed by the chief executive and its main function is to:

options.A: Co-ordinate the preparation of the functional budgets, settle differences between departments and approve the final budgets
options.B: Personally prepare every functional budget of the enterprise
options.C: Audit the actual expenditure incurred against each budget
options.D: Fix the selling prices of all products of the enterprise

e: The budget committee, headed by the chief executive, co-ordinates functional budgets, settles inter-departmental differences and approves the final budgets; it does not prepare each one itself.

q: The budget officer in a budgetary control system acts mainly as the:

options.A: Officer who sanctions all expenditure of the enterprise
options.B: Co-ordinator and secretary of the budget committee, who assembles the budgets and reports comparisons of actuals with budgets
options.C: Internal auditor of the cost accounts of the enterprise
options.D: Head of the production department for budget purposes

e: The budget officer is the co-ordinator and secretary of the budget committee, assembling budgets and reporting actuals against budgets, not the sanctioning or audit authority.

q: Before the functional budgets are prepared, the management must first determine the principal budget factor because:

options.A: It is the largest item of expenditure in the budget
options.B: It is always the availability of cash in the enterprise
options.C: All the functional budgets have to be built around the factor that limits the scale of operations
options.D: It decides the accounting period to be adopted

e: The principal budget factor is the factor limiting the scale of operations, so all functional budgets must be built around it before they are prepared.

q: In an enterprise where skilled labour of a particular grade is in short supply and output cannot be expanded beyond what that labour can produce, the principal budget factor is:

options.A: Sales demand
options.B: Plant capacity
options.C: Availability of finance
options.D: Availability of skilled labour

e: Output is limited by the scarce skilled labour, so availability of that labour, not sales demand or plant capacity, is the principal budget factor.

q: When sales demand is the principal budget factor, the budget preparation normally begins with the:

options.A: Sales budget, the other functional budgets being built upon it
options.B: Cash budget, from which the sales target is derived
options.C: Capital expenditure budget for new plant
options.D: Administrative overhead budget

e: When sales demand is the limiting factor, preparation starts with the sales budget and the other functional budgets are built upon it.

q: The production budget is normally expressed primarily in:

options.A: Money value only
options.B: Quantitative terms, that is, the number of units to be produced
options.C: Machine hours only
options.D: Percentages of installed capacity only

e: The production budget is expressed primarily in quantitative terms, the number of units to be produced, rather than only in money value.

q: The plant utilisation budget is prepared mainly to show:

options.A: The wages payable to plant operators
options.B: The historical cost of the plant installed
options.C: The extent to which the available plant and machine capacity will be used during the budget period, department by department
options.D: The depreciation to be charged on each machine

e: The plant utilisation budget shows, department by department, how far available plant and machine capacity will be used during the budget period.

q: The direct labour budget of a manufacturing enterprise sets out, for the budget period:

options.A: Only the total wages bill of the factory as a whole
options.B: The salaries of the managerial staff only
options.C: The indirect labour employed in service departments only
options.D: The labour hours and labour cost required, classified by department and by grade or type of labour

e: The direct labour budget sets out labour hours and labour cost required, classified by department and by grade or type of labour, not just a total wages bill.

q: The materials budget and the materials purchase budget differ in that the purchase budget additionally takes into account:

options.A: The opening and closing stocks of materials, so as to arrive at the quantity actually to be bought
options.B: The selling price of the finished product
options.C: The wages of the stores staff
options.D: The depreciation of the stores building

e: The purchase budget adjusts material requirements for opening and closing stocks to arrive at the quantity actually to be bought; the materials budget alone does not.

q: The production overhead budget is usefully prepared by splitting the overheads into:

options.A: Direct and indirect portions
options.B: Fixed and variable portions, so that the budget can be flexed for the actual level of activity
options.C: Controllable and non-controllable portions only
options.D: Cash and non-cash portions only

e: Splitting production overheads into fixed and variable portions lets the budget be flexed for the actual level of activity.

q: Budgeted sales of a product are 45,000 units. The opening stock of finished goods is 6,000 units and the closing stock is to be 9,000 units. The production budget for the period is:

options.A: 42,000 units
options.B: 36,000 units
options.C: 48,000 units
options.D: 45,000 units

e: Production = sales + closing stock - opening stock = 45,000 + 9,000 - 6,000 = 48,000 units.

q: Production is budgeted at 30,000 units and each unit requires 3 kg of material. The opening stock of the material is 12,000 kg and the closing stock is to be 15,000 kg. The quantity of material to be purchased is:
e: Material needed = 30,000 x 3 = 90,000 kg; purchases = 90,000 + 15,000 closing - 12,000 opening = 93,000 kg.

q: A budget for 20,000 units provides for fixed costs of Rs 3,00,000 and variable costs of Rs 45 per unit. The flexed budget allowance for an actual output of 16,000 units is:
e: Flexed cost = fixed Rs 3,00,000 + variable 45 x 16,000 = 3,00,000 + 7,20,000 = Rs 10,20,000; fixed cost does not change with output.

q: An enterprise budgets to sell 15,000 units at Rs 320 per unit. Sales returns of 500 units are expected. The budgeted net sales value is:
e: Net units sold = 15,000 - 500 returns = 14,500; budgeted net sales = 14,500 x 320 = Rs 46,40,000.

q: The selling and distribution overhead budget is prepared mainly on the basis of:

options.A: The production programme of the factory
options.B: The historical cost of the sales office building
options.C: The budgeted sales volume and the sales programme, including advertising and distribution plans
options.D: The number of shareholders of the company

e: Selling and distribution overheads are driven by budgeted sales volume and the sales programme, including advertising and distribution plans.

q: The capital expenditure budget differs from the revenue budgets mainly in that it:

options.A: Is prepared for one month at a time
options.B: Covers only items of routine maintenance
options.C: Need not be approved by higher management
options.D: Covers expenditure on fixed assets whose benefits extend over several years, and is therefore linked with long-term plans and the cash budget

e: Capital expenditure covers fixed assets whose benefits extend over several years, so it is linked with long-term plans and the cash budget, unlike routine revenue budgets.

q: The master budget, once approved by the budget committee or the board, serves as:

options.A: The authorised summary plan of the enterprise for the budget period, against which actual performance is compared
options.B: A substitute for the cash budget of the enterprise
options.C: A record of the actual results of the previous year
options.D: A budget prepared only for the finance department

e: Once approved, the master budget is the authorised summary plan of the enterprise for the period, against which actual performance is compared.

q: A fixed budget becomes unsuitable as a basis of comparison and control mainly when:

options.A: The budget period is longer than one month
options.B: The actual level of activity differs considerably from the budgeted level, so that comparing actual costs with the fixed budget costs is misleading
options.C: The enterprise prepares more than one functional budget
options.D: Fixed costs form a large part of the total cost

e: A fixed budget misleads when actual activity differs considerably from budgeted activity, because costs expected at one level are compared with costs at another level.

q: The essential prerequisite for preparing a flexible budget is that costs must first be:

options.A: Expressed only as percentages of sales
options.B: Charged wholly to the departments incurring them
options.C: Segregated into fixed, variable and semi-variable elements, the semi-variable costs being split into their fixed and variable parts
options.D: Compared with the costs of the previous year

e: Flexible budgeting first requires costs to be segregated into fixed, variable and semi-variable elements, with semi-variable costs split into fixed and variable parts.

q: In flexing a budget for the actual level of activity, the item that is NOT changed with the level of activity is:

options.A: Direct material cost
options.B: Direct labour cost
options.C: Variable production overheads
options.D: Fixed overheads, which remain at the budgeted amount within the relevant range

e: In flexing, direct materials, direct labour and variable overheads change with activity, but fixed overheads stay at the budgeted amount within the relevant range.

q: A cash budget is normally prepared for short sub-periods, such as months or weeks, chiefly in order to:

options.A: Reveal in advance the periods of cash surplus and cash shortage, so that borrowing or investment of surplus can be arranged in time
options.B: Replace the budgeted profit and loss account
options.C: Determine the selling price of the products
options.D: Ascertain the cost of production of each unit

e: Preparing a cash budget for months or weeks reveals cash surpluses and shortages in advance, so borrowing or investing surplus can be arranged in time.

q: The opening cash balance of an enterprise is Rs 50,000. Budgeted receipts are cash sales Rs 1,80,000 and collections from debtors Rs 2,70,000. Budgeted payments are to creditors Rs 2,00,000, wages Rs 1,20,000 and overheads Rs 60,000. The closing cash balance is:
Production is budgeted at 24,000 units and each unit requires 2.5 direct labour hours. The wage rate is Rs 80 per hour. The direct labour cost budget is:
e: Labour hours = 24,000 x 2.5 = 60,000 hours; direct labour cost = 60,000 x 80 = Rs 48,00,000.

q: A budget for 10,000 units shows a total cost of Rs 6,50,000, of which the fixed cost is Rs 2,50,000. The flexed budget cost for 13,000 units is:

Budgeted sales are 60,000 units, the opening stock of finished goods is 5,000 units and the closing stock is to be 8,000 units. Of the units put into production, 10% are expected to be rejected. The gross production to be budgeted is:

options.A: 70,000 units
options.B: 63,000 units
options.C: 57,000 units
options.D: 69,300 units

e: Net production needed = 60,000 + 8,000 - 5,000 = 63,000 good units; with 10 percent rejection, gross production = 63,000 / 0.90 = 70,000 units.

q: Participative (bottom-up) budgeting, under which the managers who have to work to the budget take part in setting it, has the main advantage that:

options.A: The budget can be prepared without any forecasts
options.B: The targets are more likely to be accepted and acted upon by those managers, improving motivation and commitment
options.C: No budget committee is then required
options.D: The budget figures are always lower than under top-down budgeting

e: Participative budgeting involves the managers who must work to the budget, so targets are more likely to be accepted, improving motivation and commitment.

q: 'Budgetary slack' in a budget means:

options.A: The difference between the budgeted and the actual output
options.B: The time allowed between the preparation and the approval of a budget
options.C: The deliberate understatement of expected revenue or overstatement of expected costs by a manager to make the budget easier to achieve
options.D: The surplus of cash shown by the cash budget

e: Budgetary slack is the deliberate understatement of revenue or overstatement of costs by a manager to make the budget easier to achieve.

q: A budget is normally revised during the budget period when:

options.A: A small variance appears in any one month
options.B: The manager of a department asks for a revision
options.C: The accounting period comes to an end
options.D: Circumstances change fundamentally, for example a major change in prices, demand or the principal budget factor, so that the original budget ceases to be a realistic basis of control

e: A budget is revised mid-period only when circumstances change fundamentally, such as major price, demand or principal-factor changes, making the original budget unrealistic for control.

q: In zero-base budgeting, the activities of each department are analysed in terms of:

options.A: Decision packages, each describing the purpose, cost, benefit and consequences of not performing the activity
options.B: Percentages of the previous year's expenditure
options.C: Fixed percentages laid down by the finance department
options.D: The personal estimates of the departmental head alone

e: Zero-base budgeting analyses each activity through decision packages describing purpose, cost, benefits and the consequences of not performing the activity.

q: In zero-base budgeting, after the decision packages have been prepared, they are:

options.A: Approved automatically in the order in which they are received
options.B: Ranked in order of priority by management, and funds are allocated down the ranking until the available resources are exhausted
options.C: Sent to the auditors for certification
options.D: Consolidated without any evaluation of their benefits

e: Decision packages are ranked in order of priority and funds are allocated down the ranking until available resources are exhausted.

q: A limitation of zero-base budgeting is that it:

options.A: Ignores the benefits of the activities it examines
options.B: Can be applied only to capital expenditure
options.C: Is time-consuming and costly to operate, involves heavy paperwork and may over-emphasise short-term measurable benefits
options.D: Does not require any justification of expenditure

e: Zero-base budgeting is time-consuming and costly, involves heavy paperwork and may over-emphasise short-term measurable benefits.

q: Performance budgeting, as applied in government, lays its main emphasis on:

options.A: The objects of expenditure, such as salaries and stores, alone
options.B: Economy in the purchase of inputs alone
options.C: The classification of expenditure by the department incurring it alone
options.D: Accomplishments and work programmes, relating the financial outlay to physical targets, activities and programmes

e: Performance budgeting emphasises accomplishments and work programmes, relating financial outlay to physical targets, activities and programmes, not just objects of expenditure.

q: A distinguishing feature of performance budgeting is that expenditure is classified by:

options.A: Functions, programmes, activities and projects, instead of only by objects of expenditure
options.B: The source from which the funds are received
options.C: The grade of the officer incurring the expenditure
options.D: The month in which the expenditure is incurred

e: Performance budgeting classifies expenditure by functions, programmes, activities and projects instead of only by objects of expenditure.

q: For performance budgeting to work effectively, an essential supporting requirement is:

options.A: Abolition of the object-wise classification of expenditure
options.B: The development of suitable work measurement, unit costs and physical performance norms for the activities undertaken
options.C: Preparation of the budget for ten years at a time
options.D: Exemption of the programmes from any financial review

e: Performance budgeting needs suitable work measurement, unit costs and physical performance norms for the activities undertaken to link money with results.

q: Programme budgeting (planning-programming-budgeting) is distinguished from ordinary annual budgeting by its emphasis on:

options.A: Line items of expenditure for a single year
options.B: The personal requirements of each office
options.C: Long-term objectives, identification of alternative programmes to achieve them, and systematic analysis of their costs and benefits over several years
options.D: The cash position from week to week

e: Programme budgeting stresses long-term objectives, alternative programmes to achieve them and systematic cost-benefit analysis over several years, not single-year line items.
